pamphlet_excerpts: General Knowledge: The history of animation is as old as the history of story telling (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 2: The word animate means "alive." When early humans first painted animals and hunting scenes on cave walls, they lit fires to show off their work (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 3: The dancing flames cast irregular light in the caves, making the images of prehistoric animals appear to be alive and moving (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 4: Also, from the earliest times, children worldwide have used a light source to project hand shadows onto a wall to create the shapes of animals (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (General Knowledge): This kind of entertainment can be enjoyed by a group of friends (p. 21).
Step 2 (General Knowledge): The shared experience of creating lifelike imitation is a key part of the attraction of animation (p. 21).
Step 3 (General Knowledge): The idea of projecting shadows led to the first magic lantern shows, starting around the mid to late 1700s and lasting until the introduction (p. 21).
Step 4 (General Knowledge): A primitive projection device like a wooden box with a candle inside was fitted with a lens (p. 21).

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles of Animation: The principles of animation are a set of 12 basic ideas applied to animation to create appealing, believable results (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 2: They were introduced by two of the original Disney animators, Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas, in their book, Disney Animation: The Illusion (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 3: Since that time, the principles have become standard in the animation industry (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 4: Straight Ahead Action and Pose to Pose Straight-ahead action and pose to pose are the two main methods for animating (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Principles of Animation): Using straight-ahead action, the animator draws or animates frame by frame, doing the drawings in order: 1, 2, 3, 4 (p. 35).
Step 2 (Principles of Animation): With pose-to-pose animation, in contrast, the animator draws or poses the main (key) frames of the animation before filling in the in-between (p. 35).
Step 3 (Principles of Animation): Using the pose-to-pose method, the animator might do drawing 1, then drawing 25, and then drawing 47, before going back to do the drawings (p. 35).
Step 4 (Principles of Animation): Most animators use the pose-to-pose method because it offers benefits in timing and frame composition (p. 35).
